paragraphs: Low-rank matrix estimation seeks a compact matrix description that still explains the data. The Schatten-p quasi-norm encourages this structure and can offer benefits over convex alternatives, but its nonconvex optimization is computationally demanding. This paper develops a different mathematical expression for the penalty, using smaller matrices whose product represents the matrix being estimated.

The new expression works for every continuous choice of p between zero and one, including one, and separates across columns of the factors. It encourages groups of factor entries to disappear together, imposing low rank through group sparsity. This structure enables algorithms that avoid singular value decomposition, reducing computational complexity relative to working directly with the original penalty.

The analysis connects local minima of the factorized surrogate to local minima of the original problem. For squared Frobenius loss and linear operators satisfying the restricted isometry property, the authors also propose rank-one updates that offer an escape from poor local minima. Matrix-completion experiments demonstrate efficiency, complementing the mathematical justification for the reformulation.
neurips-2020-a-novel-variational-form-of.tldr: A factorized Schatten-p penalty enables cheaper low-rank optimization while connecting surrogate local minima to those of the original problem.

paragraphs: Observational data can leave several causal graphs indistinguishable, making interventions necessary to determine edge directions. This paper studies intervention design when the observational equivalence class is already supplied. Its setting assumes no hidden confounders, selection bias, or feedback, and assumes interventions are noiseless.

The main theoretical contribution strengthens what large cliques imply about difficulty. Earlier worst-case bounds showed that a large fully connected group could make learning difficult. The authors instead establish a lower bound applying to every graph in the equivalence class. Using directed clique trees, they decompose the graph into independently orientable pieces and show that required single-node interventions are at least the sum of half the largest clique size in each chain component.

They also develop a two-phase intervention strategy. Under specified conditions on the chordal skeleton, its intervention count is within a logarithmic factor of optimal, measured in the number of maximal cliques. Synthetic experiments report scaling to larger graphs than most related methods and better worst-case performance than other scalable approaches.
neurips-2020-active-structure-learning-o.tldr: Directed clique trees reveal a universal intervention lower bound and support an efficient, conditionally near-optimal causal discovery strategy.

paragraphs: Face-forgery detectors benefit from varied, challenging training examples. This paper addresses a specific gap: identity-swapping methods struggle when faces differ substantially in illumination or skin color. Producing convincing swaps across these appearance differences requires transferring fine details while retaining the intended identity traits.

The proposed Appearance Optimal Transport model treats appearance mapping as a transport problem in both learned feature space and pixel space. A relighting generator approximates the transport plan by minimizing Wasserstein distance between learned features. The authors report that this learned approach provides better performance with less computation than conventional optimization.

A second component refines the mapping at the pixel level through a segmentation game. Its discriminator identifies fake regions within mixtures of real and generated image patches, supporting further reduction of the pixel-space Wasserstein distance. Experiments report improvements over competing identity-swapping methods and show that the generated examples improve face-forgery detection. The contribution therefore connects better handling of appearance differences during generation with more useful training data for detectors.
neurips-2020-aot-appearance-optimal-tran.tldr: AOT uses optimal transport to generate identity swaps across large appearance differences and improve face-forgery detector training.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization aims to find good solutions using relatively few evaluations of an objective. BoTorch provides a programming framework for this process, with applications including automated machine learning, engineering, and experimental design. Its focus is making sophisticated probabilistic decision rules practical to implement and optimize.

The framework combines acquisition functions evaluated through Monte Carlo sampling with sample average approximation, automatic differentiation, and variance reduction. Sample average approximation supplies a sampled optimization objective that can be handled with deterministic optimization. Fast predictive distributions and hardware acceleration make this foundation practical, while a modular PyTorch design supports flexible probabilistic models and new acquisition functions.

The work includes theoretical convergence results and a new one-shot formulation of the Knowledge Gradient acquisition strategy. These contributions connect the software design to the underlying optimization methods, rather than treating implementation as a separate concern. Experiments show improved sample efficiency relative to other popular libraries, indicating that the framework can make better use of objective evaluations in the tested settings.
neurips-2020-botorch-a-framework-for-eff.tldr: BoTorch combines Monte Carlo acquisition functions, efficient optimization, and modular software to improve Bayesian optimization’s sample efficiency.

paragraphs: Understanding graph convolutional networks becomes difficult when graphs are large and comparisons depend on discrete structures such as node correspondences. This paper studies them through random graph models in which each node has a latent variable and edges are sampled according to a similarity kernel. That setup provides an underlying geometric description of the graph.

The authors first analyze how a graph convolutional network approaches a continuous counterpart as the number of nodes increases. Their results are non-asymptotic, so they concern finite graph sizes rather than only an infinite-size limit. They also cover relatively sparse graphs whose average degree increases logarithmically with the number of nodes.

The second contribution examines stability when the underlying random graph model undergoes small deformations. Working in the continuous description allows changes to be measured geometrically, offering a more intuitive account than purely discrete comparisons. Together, the results connect finite graph computations to continuous representations and provide a framework for understanding how sensitive those computations are to changes in the graph-generating model.
neurips-2020-convergence-and-stability-o.tldr: The paper connects GCNs on large random graphs to continuous models and analyzes their convergence and stability under geometric deformations.

paragraphs: Early in training, a convolutional network can propagate noisy, distorted information through its internal features. This paper proposes a curriculum that controls the detail available inside the network as learning progresses. The aim is to let the model learn from smoother representations before exposing it to more high-frequency information.

The method applies a Gaussian filter to the output feature map of each convolutional layer. Initially, stronger smoothing suppresses high-frequency content. Decreasing the Gaussian kernel’s variance over training gradually permits more of that content to pass through. The curriculum therefore operates on intermediate representations, directly changing what information later computations receive.

The authors report that this progressive increase in detail helps networks learn better representations and improves performance across several vision tasks and architectures. The scheme introduces neither additional trainable parameters nor an auxiliary regularization objective. Reported gains include transfer learning, transfer across tasks, and generative modeling, supporting the usefulness of smoothing as an augmentation to training across the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-curriculum-by-smoothing-eff.tldr: Gradually reducing smoothing inside CNNs creates a training curriculum that improves visual representations without adding trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Choosing neural-network hyperparameters can be viewed as a nested optimization problem: network parameters are optimized within a broader search over hyperparameters. Self-Tuning Networks use a hypernetwork to amortize the inner optimization. This paper identifies training pathologies in that approach and develops an architecture intended to make the process more stable and efficient.

Delta-STN changes what the hypernetwork must approximate accurately. Instead of concentrating on the entire best-response function, which describes optimized network parameters across hyperparameter choices, it focuses on the best-response Jacobian. This Jacobian describes how those parameters respond locally to hyperparameter changes. The method obtains this focus by reparameterizing the hypernetwork and linearizing the network around its current parameters.

Experiments evaluate tuning regularization choices such as weight decay, dropout, and the number of cutout holes. The authors report higher accuracy, faster convergence, and improved stability compared with existing approaches. These findings support the practical value of approximating local response information carefully, rather than requiring an equally accurate approximation of the full parameter-response function.
neurips-2020-delta-stn-efficient-bilevel.tldr: Delta-STN improves hyperparameter tuning by focusing its hypernetwork on local parameter responses, yielding faster and more stable optimization in experiments.

paragraphs: Median-based distributed optimization offers useful properties: signSGD with majority voting reduces communication through one-bit gradient compression, while medianSGD was proposed for robustness against Byzantine workers. Their convergence analyses, however, rely heavily on workers receiving independent data from the same distribution. Federated settings often violate that assumption because users have different data.

This paper analyzes what happens under such heterogeneity. It identifies a mismatch between the expected median and mean of local gradients as a source of non-convergence. The distinction matters because aggregating workers through a median need not produce the direction represented by their mean when their data distributions differ.

The proposed correction perturbs local gradients with noise. The authors prove that this mechanism can close the mean–median gap and establish convergence to stationary solutions for the resulting methods. The correction largely retains desirable properties such as signSGD’s low communication cost per iteration. Beyond distributed training, the technique may also help when a median estimator is used to estimate a mean.
neurips-2020-distributed-training-with-h.tldr: Noise-based gradient correction closes a mean–median mismatch that can prevent median-based distributed training from converging on heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph completion uses models to infer missing relationships. Tensor-factorization approaches are powerful for this task, but the paper identifies serious overfitting as a recurring problem. Regularizers can restrain that tendency, yet existing choices such as squared Frobenius and tensor nuclear norm penalties have limited applicability across methods.

The proposed Duality-Induced Regularizer, or DURA, builds on a relationship between two ways of modeling the same completion problem. A tensor-factorization model often has a closely associated model based on distances. The paper calls the factorization model the primal and its distance-based counterpart the dual, and uses this connection as the basis for regularization.

The stated contribution combines improved performance with broad applicability to existing factorization methods. This matters because a useful regularizer must fit the models people actually use, alongside controlling overfitting. The central insight is that an associated distance-based formulation can guide the regularization of a factorization model. The abstract presents this relationship as occurring often, rather than asserting that every possible factorization model has such a counterpart.
neurips-2020-duality-induced-regularizer.tldr: DURA uses connections between tensor-factorization and distance-based models to regularize knowledge graph completion across a broad range of methods.

paragraphs: A classifier can assign high confidence to an input that differs substantially from its training data. This makes ordinary softmax confidence an unreliable signal for detecting out-of-distribution inputs. The paper proposes using an energy score to distinguish familiar inputs from unfamiliar ones more effectively.

The framework supports two uses. Energy can score inputs using an already trained neural classifier, or it can serve as a training cost that explicitly shapes the energy surface for detection. The authors show a theoretical alignment between energy scores and input probability density, and argue that this makes the scores less vulnerable to the overconfidence problem affecting softmax.

For a WideResNet pretrained on CIFAR-10, the abstract reports an 18.03% reduction in average false-positive rate at a true-positive rate of 95% compared with softmax confidence. Energy-based training also outperforms the state of the art on the evaluated common benchmarks. These findings support both a scoring-only route and a training-based route to better detection, without implying that unfamiliar inputs are always identified correctly.
neurips-2020-energy-based-out-of-distrib.tldr: Energy scores improve out-of-distribution detection and can be used either with pretrained classifiers or as an explicit training objective.

paragraphs: Standard transformer attention becomes expensive on long sequences because its computation grows quadratically with sequence length. This paper reduces that cost by sharing attention calculations among groups of queries. The goal is to retain useful attention behavior while spending less computation on separate query-by-key comparisons.

Clustered attention groups queries and computes attention for each cluster’s centroid. It then improves this approximation by using the clusters to identify keys receiving high attention for each query and calculating those query–key dot products exactly. With the number of clusters fixed, the resulting computation grows linearly with sequence length.

On two speech-recognition datasets, the method consistently outperforms standard transformers at a given computational budget. The authors also approximate a pretrained BERT model on GLUE and SQuAD using only 25 clusters, reporting no loss of performance. These results show that shared coarse attention, supplemented with targeted exact calculations, can preserve detailed attention behavior in the evaluated tasks while reducing the cost of handling longer sequences.
neurips-2020-fast-transformers-with-clus.tldr: Clustered attention shares computations across queries and selectively refines them, achieving linear sequence-length complexity for a fixed cluster count.

paragraphs: Market equilibria are useful in settings such as digital advertising, fair division, and resource sharing. For several utility models, finding an equilibrium can be expressed as convex optimization. This paper develops simple first-order algorithms suited to large markets, focusing on linear, quasilinear, and Leontief utilities.

The authors exploit each market’s structure to rewrite its convex program as smooth optimization over a set defined by linear constraints. They establish linear convergence for projected gradient using weaker conditions than standard strong convexity and refine relevant convergence constants. They also prove linear convergence for proximal gradient with a practical line search under the Proximal-PL condition.

For quasilinear utilities, a new convex formulation supports mirror descent with sublinear convergence of the final iterate. It also produces a version of Proportional Response dynamics, extending an interpretable method originally developed for linear utilities. Numerical experiments suggest a practical distinction: Proportional Response efficiently obtains approximate equilibria, while projected gradient with line search can be much faster when greater accuracy is required.
neurips-2020-first-order-methods-for-lar.tldr: Structured convex reformulations yield efficient first-order market-equilibrium algorithms with convergence guarantees and different advantages at different accuracy levels.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning divides decision-making between a high-level policy that chooses subgoals and a low-level policy that pursues them. When the high-level policy can choose from a very large goal space, both selecting goals and learning to reach them become difficult. This paper addresses that search burden by restricting which subgoals are considered.

The proposed adjacency constraint limits high-level choices to a region reachable within k steps of the current state. A learned adjacency network distinguishes nearby subgoals from non-adjacent ones, making the restriction practical to implement. This narrows the high-level action space and simplifies the subgoal choices presented to the low-level learner.

The authors prove that the restriction preserves an optimal hierarchical policy in deterministic Markov decision processes. Experiments on discrete and continuous control tasks show improved performance when the constraint is added to leading hierarchical methods. Those empirical gains occur in both deterministic and stochastic environments; the policy-preservation theorem specifically applies to the deterministic setting. The results connect a smaller search space with more effective hierarchical learning.
neurips-2020-generating-adjacency-constr.tldr: Restricting hierarchical subgoals to a learned k-step neighborhood improves learning and preserves optimal hierarchical policies in deterministic environments.

paragraphs: Tasks such as understanding a story require current decisions to depend on earlier information. Hebbian synaptic plasticity is believed to support memory retention in the brain, but how it combines with ongoing cortical computation remains unclear. This paper explores that connection through a simple neural-network model called a Hebbian Memory Network.

At the model’s core is a hetero-associative network whose connections change through Hebbian plasticity. This core stores associations between different stimuli. The authors show that the surrounding network can be optimized to use those changing connections in its computations, linking the act of storing an association to its later use in a decision.

H-Mems can memorize a stimulus-pair association after a single presentation and use it later. They also solve demanding question-answering tasks involving synthetic stories. These demonstrations establish that simple Hebbian plasticity can provide useful memory within an optimized neural model. They support a computational role for plasticity-driven associations, while the reported story-understanding evidence concerns the synthetic tasks used in the study.
neurips-2020-h-mem-harnessing-synaptic-p.tldr: Hebbian Memory Networks learn to use plastic connections for one-shot associative memory and later decisions, including synthetic story question answering.

paragraphs: Predicting visual neurons’ responses to natural images requires models that learn from limited neural recordings. Deep networks are promising, but their data needs can far exceed what recording sessions provide. This paper asks whether carefully chosen training images can make each available example more useful for learning a predictive model.

The proposed images are high-contrast, binarized transformations of natural images, called gaudy images. They exaggerate visual features rather than preserving the original range of image values. The authors use these images to train networks that predict higher-order visual cortical responses, while retaining prediction on natural images as the target.

Simulation experiments and analyses of real neural data show that gaudy images substantially reduce the number of training images needed for accurate natural-image response prediction. Images selected this way before training also outperform images selected during training by the evaluated active-learning algorithms. The findings suggest that emphasizing particular natural-image features can improve training efficiency. The authors view better cortical modeling and new questions about visual processing as potential future benefits.
neurips-2020-high-contrast-gaudy-images-.tldr: High-contrast, binarized training images reduce the data needed to train networks that predict visual cortical responses to natural images.

paragraphs: Many neural implicit surface representations depend on separating inside from outside, which requires closed surfaces. Real scanned scenes and objects can contain open walls, clothing, or internal structures. Artificially closing such surfaces can create artifacts. This paper proposes a representation that avoids requiring that inside–outside distinction.

Neural Distance Fields predict unsigned distance to a surface from sparse point clouds. Because the distance does not encode a side of the surface, the representation accommodates open shapes while retaining continuous, high-resolution outputs. The authors show how to extract dense point clouds and meshes, calculate surface normals, and render the representation with a modified sphere-tracing procedure.

ShapeNet experiments report state-of-the-art performance and demonstrate reconstruction of internal geometry, including chairs inside a bus. The paper also explores multi-target regression using techniques drawn from graphics rendering. Its scope extends beyond three-dimensional objects: the authors show approximation of more general open surfaces, including curves, manifolds, and functions. The contribution broadens the geometry a learned implicit representation can express.
neurips-2020-neural-unsigned-distance-fi.tldr: Neural unsigned distance fields represent high-resolution open surfaces and internal geometry without requiring objects to be artificially closed.

paragraphs: Adversarial training changes the optimization problem a model must solve. This paper examines how allowing adversarial perturbations of different sizes changes the loss landscape. Its central concern is why stronger adversarial training can become difficult to optimize, even before considering the quality of the resulting model.

Analytical studies show increased curvature and more scattered gradients in the adversarial loss landscape. Numerical analyses support this account: large adversarial budgets hinder escape from unfavorable random initializations, produce gradients that do not vanish, and lead to sharper minima. Together, these findings identify concrete optimization difficulties associated with the strength of the adversary.

The authors respond with periodic adversarial scheduling, or PAS, which schedules adversarial training periodically. They report that this strategy can overcome the identified challenges, improve results relative to vanilla adversarial training, and substantially reduce sensitivity to learning-rate choice. The contribution connects an analysis of training geometry with a practical scheduling intervention. Its findings support adjusting the adversarial training schedule as a way to improve the optimization process.
neurips-2020-on-the-loss-landscape-of-ad.tldr: The paper links adversarial training to harder loss landscapes and proposes periodic scheduling that improves optimization and reduces learning-rate sensitivity.

paragraphs: Gaussian process models often require approximate probabilistic inference. Common methods optimize divergences such as Kullback–Leibler divergence, partly because they are technically convenient. This paper develops Quantile Propagation, which instead uses the L2 Wasserstein distance, a metric that incorporates the geometry of the underlying sample space.

The method resembles expectation propagation but changes what is matched during approximation. Expectation propagation matches moments, whereas Quantile Propagation matches quantile functions, which describe values at different probability levels. The authors show that its mean update is the same as expectation propagation’s, while its variance update is smaller. This helps alleviate expectation propagation’s tendency to overestimate posterior variances.

Using Wasserstein distance introduces technical complexity, but the method retains expectation propagation’s favorable locality property. That allows efficient updates without abandoning the new distance measure. Experiments on classification and Poisson regression report better performance than both expectation propagation and variational Bayes. The findings show that changing the geometry of approximation can improve inference while preserving a computational structure that makes the method practical.
neurips-2020-quantile-propagation-for-wa.tldr: Quantile Propagation uses Wasserstein distance for efficient Gaussian process inference and reduces expectation propagation’s tendency to overestimate uncertainty.

paragraphs: Estimating an individual treatment effect requires reasoning about outcomes under alternative treatments. A generative model’s predictive objective may not adequately address causal issues such as covariate imbalance or the inability to directly validate unobserved counterfactuals. This paper develops a Bayesian generative framework designed specifically around causal effect estimation.

The framework combines representation learning, adversarial matching, and causal estimation. Using the Robinson decomposition, the authors reformulate a variational bound so that it targets treatment effects rather than particular predictive goals. They also account for uncertainty in the learned representation and use a Fenchel minimax game to address imbalance between representations.

New theory supports the representation-balancing procedure’s role in counterfactual generalization. The latent-variable formulation also enables robustness to unobserved confounders, broadening the proposed framework’s applicability. Tests against competing methods across simulations and real-world datasets produce encouraging results. The work’s central message is that generative estimation can be made more relevant to causal questions by changing its objective and explicitly handling representation uncertainty and imbalance.
neurips-2020-reconsidering-generative-ob.tldr: A generative Bayesian framework targets treatment-effect estimation directly while addressing representation imbalance, uncertainty, and unobserved confounding.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains across users while keeping their samples on their devices. Differences between users’ data distributions can nevertheless hurt the shared model. This paper focuses on structured affine shifts, including device-related image differences in intensity, contrast, and brightness, as a model of that heterogeneity.

The proposed FLRA framework trains against affine Wasserstein shifts of the observed sample distribution. It casts robust learning as a distributed minimax problem and provides an efficient gradient descent–ascent method to solve it. The authors establish convergence and performance guarantees, along with generalization bounds connecting the empirical sample distribution to the underlying distribution.

Numerical experiments show that affine shifts alone can substantially reduce a learned classifier’s performance on a new test user. In those experiments, FLRA delivers significant gains over standard federated learning and adversarial training methods. The results make a concrete case for modeling device-dependent transformations during federated training. The robustness claim concerns the specified affine shift model, giving the guarantees a defined scope.
neurips-2020-robust-federated-learning-t.tldr: FLRA provides federated learning robust to modeled affine distribution shifts, with optimization guarantees and improved performance on shifted test users.

paragraphs: Constituency parsing organizes a sentence into a syntax tree. Transition-based parsers build that structure through a sequence of actions, but the commonly used shift-reduce system differs from the strongly incremental behavior suggested by psycholinguistic research. This paper develops a parser that maintains one growing tree and incorporates exactly one token at each step.

Its attach-juxtapose transition system defines how each new token enters the existing partial tree. A graph neural network encodes that tree, and the parser uses the encoding to predict its next action. The design therefore makes the currently assembled syntax structure directly available when deciding how to extend the parse.

On Penn Treebank, the parser outperforms existing parsers trained only with constituency trees and matches leading parsers that additionally use dependency-tree training data. On Chinese Treebank, it establishes a new state of the art. These results show that the proposed incremental constraint is compatible with strong parsing accuracy, while providing a tree-building process motivated by evidence about human sentence processing.
neurips-2020-strongly-incremental-consti.tldr: An attach-juxtapose parser uses graph neural networks to grow one syntax tree token by token while achieving strong benchmark accuracy.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes depend on a kernel that reflects the structure of the data. Selecting its hyperparameters often requires repeated marginal-likelihood evaluations, each involving a linear-system solve. This search can dominate practical computation. The paper replaces that repeated fitting procedure with a neural network trained to infer kernel properties from regression data.

The network amortizes inference: training creates a reusable estimator that can serve different tasks. Its hierarchical self-attention architecture handles datasets with different numbers of examples and input dimensions. The resulting hyperparameter estimates are invariant to reordering either data points or dimensions, so arbitrary presentation order does not change the inferred kernel.

A single network trained on synthetic data transfers directly to several previously unseen real-world Gaussian process applications. Experiments report hyperparameter quality comparable to conventional model-selection procedures, with substantially faster estimation. This accelerates regression and related applications such as Bayesian optimization and Bayesian quadrature. The findings support moving expensive hyperparameter-inference work into a shared training phase for the evaluated range of tasks.
neurips-2020-task-agnostic-amortized-inf.tldr: A reusable attention network estimates Gaussian process kernel hyperparameters much faster than conventional fitting while achieving comparable quality in experiments.

paragraphs: Neural-network verification often replaces difficult neuron behavior with convex approximations that are easier to analyze. This paper strengthens those approximations for ReLU neurons. Its key move is to retain the multiple inputs to the affine computation preceding a ReLU, rather than considering only the resulting single scalar input.

Using submodularity and convex geometry, the authors characterize the tightest convex relaxation when those multivariate inputs lie in a box domain. This relaxation is substantially stronger than the usual scalar-input version. Although its description can contain exponentially many inequalities, a linear-time separation procedure identifies needed constraints, allowing optimization algorithms to incorporate them as required.

The paper builds two polynomial-time verification algorithms from this result. One uses linear programming to exploit the complete relaxation; the other provides a fast propagation approach that generalizes existing methods. Both verify substantially more instances than comparable algorithms for a modest increase in computational effort. The findings show that a purported barrier for single-neuron relaxations can be improved by retaining richer information about each neuron’s inputs.
neurips-2020-the-convex-relaxation-barri.tldr: Stronger multivariate ReLU relaxations let verification algorithms certify more instances with only a modest increase in computation.

paragraphs: Zero-shot semantic segmentation assigns pixel labels for categories that have no training examples. Many approaches transfer knowledge through relationships between visual features and semantic information. This paper focuses on a problem within the seen categories: noisy samples and outliers can damage the representations that later support transfer to unseen classes.

The proposed framework uses Bayesian uncertainty estimation to distinguish unreliable training samples. It models network outputs with Gaussian and Laplacian distributions, whose variances represent observation noise and input uncertainty. Those estimated variances enter the learning objectives as adaptive attenuation, changing how strongly individual samples influence training.

As a result, the model gives more attention to representative examples and reduces the influence of noisy or outlying ones. The intended benefit is a more reliable basis for generalizing to novel categories. Experiments across multiple challenging benchmarks report significant accuracy improvements over previous approaches for large open-set segmentation. The contribution links uncertainty estimates to training decisions, showing their usefulness for improving transfer beyond the classes observed during learning.
neurips-2020-uncertainty-aware-learning-.tldr: Uncertainty-based weighting reduces the influence of noisy seen-class samples and improves segmentation accuracy on unseen categories.

paragraphs: Continuous-time event prediction must determine both what happens next and when it happens. Such sequences appear in behavioral records, transactions, and medical data. Existing neural models commonly treat all sequences as coming from the same distribution, although different users or sources can exhibit substantially different behavior.

This paper extends neural marked point process models with a latent variable encoding user characteristics. A mixture of latent embeddings represents variation in user behavior, with mixture components modeling characteristic traits. The model is trained through amortized variational inference, providing a learned inference mechanism for the latent representation within the event-sequence framework.

Evaluation on four large real-world datasets shows systematic improvements over existing work across several predictive measures. These include log-likelihood, ranking the next event, and identifying a sequence’s source. The range of improvements suggests that representing user differences benefits both event prediction and recognition of who generated a sequence. The contribution makes source-dependent variation part of the model rather than relying on a single shared distribution to explain all observed event histories.
neurips-2020-user-dependent-neural-seque.tldr: Latent user embeddings improve neural continuous-time event models by explicitly representing differences between the sources of event sequences.
